topics.title: React Native vs React for the web — what actually differs?
topics.html:
Same React: same hooks, same state, same reconciliation, same component model. What changes is what React renders into — real native views instead of DOM nodes.

React (web)React Native
OutputDOM nodes (div, span)Real native views (UIView on iOS, ViewGroup on Android)
Building blocksAny HTML tagView, Text, Image, ScrollView, TextInput, Pressable
StylingCSS files, cascade, inheritanceJS objects, no cascade, no inheritance, subset of CSS
Layout defaultdisplay:block, flexDirection:rowEverything is flex, flexDirection: "column"
Unitspx, rem, %, vhUnitless density-independent numbers (+ % in some props)
NavigationURL + historyA navigation library holding a stack of screens
ShippingDeploy and it is liveApp Store / Play review, or an OTA update for JS-only changes
  • There is no DOM. No document, no window, no querySelector, no localStorage. Libraries that touch the DOM simply will not work.
  • Every piece of text must sit inside <Text>. A bare string inside a <View> is a crash, not a warning.
  • No :hover, no media queries, no CSS classes. Conditional styles are just JavaScript: arrays of style objects and ternaries.
  • What stays exactly the same: hooks, context, Redux/Zustand/React Query, TypeScript, most of your business logic, and the way you think about components.
// web
<div className="card" onClick={open}>
  Hello
</div>

// native
<Pressable style={styles.card} onPress={open}>
  <Text>Hello</Text>
</Pressable>

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  card: { padding: 16, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#fff" },
});
💬 Say it like this

React Native is the same React, but the renderer is different. On the web React produces DOM nodes; in React Native it produces real native views — a real UIView on iOS and a real Android view. So my components, hooks, state and data layer look exactly like a web project, and what I have to relearn is the platform: the set of primitives is small, styling is a JavaScript object with a subset of CSS, and there is no cascade or inheritance.

The practical difference in daily work is that I cannot use any library that touches the DOM, and I have to think about two operating systems at once — keyboard behaviour, back button, safe areas and permissions all differ.

Is React Native a WebView?
No. That is Cordova/Ionic. React Native creates real native views; the JavaScript only describes what the UI should look like. A WebView is one component you can use, not how the app is built.
Can you share code between web and native?
Business logic, types, API layer, state stores and hooks — yes, in a monorepo package. UI components — mostly no, unless you use react-native-web and accept its constraints. The realistic split is "share the core, write the screens twice".
React Native vs Flutter, in one sentence?
React Native uses real platform views and JavaScript; Flutter draws everything itself with its own engine and Dart. RN wins on team skills and native look; Flutter wins on pixel-identical UI across platforms.

topics.title: How does JavaScript talk to native? The old Bridge architecture.
topics.html:
This is the "legacy" architecture, but interviewers still ask it because it explains why the New Architecture exists.

┌───────────── JS thread ─────────────┐ │ your React code, Hermes/JSC │ └──────────────┬──────────────────────┘ │ the BRIDGE │ async · batched · JSON strings ┌──────────────┴──────────────────────┐ │ Native side: UI thread + modules │ │ creates real UIView / ViewGroup │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘
  • The two worlds never share memory. Every call is serialized to JSON, put in a queue, batched, and delivered asynchronously to the other side.
  • Consequences you can name in an interview: everything is async (you cannot read a native value synchronously), there is a serialization cost on every message, and the queue can get congested — that is why a fast scroll shows blank cells, or a JS-driven animation stutters.
  • All native modules were created at startup, whether you used them or not, which made the app start slower as it grew.
  • Native code had no types coming from JS — a wrong argument type was found at runtime, often as a crash.
The classic follow-up: "Why do I see blank areas when I scroll a long list fast?" Because the new rows are rendered on the JS thread and their instructions still have to cross the bridge. The native scroll itself runs at 60 FPS on the UI thread, so the scroll is smooth — but the content is late.
💬 Say it like this

In the old architecture JavaScript and native code lived on separate threads and could only exchange JSON messages over something called the bridge. It was asynchronous and batched, so nothing was ever instant, and everything had to be serialized first.

That single design choice explains most of the old performance problems: blank cells in a fast scroll, stuttering animations driven from JS, and a slow cold start because every native module was initialised up front. The New Architecture was built specifically to remove that bottleneck.

If the bridge is async, how do native animations stay smooth?
With useNativeDriver: true the whole animation description is sent to native once, and then it runs on the UI thread every frame without touching JS. That is why it survives a busy JS thread.
Does the bridge still exist today?
Only through an interop layer for old third-party libraries. In the New Architecture the JSON bridge is replaced by JSI, which lets JS call C++ directly.

topics.title: The New Architecture — JSI, TurboModules, Fabric, Codegen.
topics.html:
Four parts. Learn them as one story: JSI is the new road, everything else drives on it.

PieceWhat it isWhat it fixes
JSIA thin C++ layer that lets JavaScript hold a reference to a native object and call its methods directlyNo JSON, no queue. Calls can be synchronous. This is the foundation of the other three.
TurboModulesThe new way to write native modules, built on JSIModules are loaded lazily, on first use → faster startup. Methods can be sync and are type-safe.
FabricThe new renderer, with the view tree living in C++Layout and view creation are faster, the tree is shared, and it supports concurrent React — Suspense, transitions, startTransition.
CodegenA build step that reads your TypeScript spec files and generates the C++/Java/ObjC glueType mismatches between JS and native become build errors instead of runtime crashes.
  • It has been on by default since RN 0.76 (late 2024). Interviewers like asking "is it still opt-in?" — the answer is no.
  • Fabric keeps three trees: the React element tree, the shadow tree (C++, where layout is computed) and the real native view tree. Updates can be applied in one synchronous commit.
  • Because the renderer can now render synchronously when needed, React 18/19 features actually behave correctly — for example a transition can be interrupted, and useLayoutEffect measurements are reliable.
  • The real migration pain is not your code — it is third-party libraries that were never updated. Old modules run through an interop layer, but some break, especially ones with custom native views.
// A TurboModule spec — this file is the contract. Codegen reads it.
// NativeDeviceInfo.ts
import type { TurboModule } from "react-native";
import { TurboModuleRegistry } from "react-native";

export interface Spec extends TurboModule {
  getBatteryLevel(): number;        // can be synchronous now
  getDeviceName(): Promise<string>;
}

export default TurboModuleRegistry.getEnforcing<Spec>("DeviceInfo");
💬 Say it like this

The New Architecture replaces the JSON bridge with JSI, which is a C++ layer that lets JavaScript hold a direct reference to a native object and call it like a normal function — no serialization, and synchronously if needed.

On top of JSI there are three things. TurboModules are native modules that load lazily on first use, so the app starts faster. Fabric is the new renderer that keeps the view tree in C++, which makes layout faster and finally makes concurrent React work properly on mobile. And Codegen generates the glue code from TypeScript specs, so a wrong type is a build error instead of a crash on a user's phone.

In practice, since 0.76 it is the default. The migration work in a real project is mostly checking that every native dependency supports it.

What is a "shadow tree"?
A lightweight copy of the UI tree used to compute layout with Yoga before touching real views. In the old architecture it lived on a separate background thread in Java/ObjC; in Fabric it is C++ and shared by both sides.
How do you check if the New Architecture is on?
global.nativeFabricUIManager is defined when Fabric is active, and the build flags are newArchEnabled=true in gradle.properties and RCT_NEW_ARCH_ENABLED=1 for iOS.
Did it make apps faster automatically?
Startup and list scrolling usually improve, but it is not magic. If your screen is slow because of too many re-renders or huge images, the New Architecture will not save you.

topics.title: Walk me through the whole React Native architecture.
topics.html:
One picture, five layers. Read it top to bottom — that is the direction one update travels.

Layer by layer, in plain words:

LayerWhat lives thereWhy you care
JS threadHermes runtime, React itself, the reconciler, and all your app logic — hooks, Redux/Zustand, fetch calls, navigationThis is the thread you block. Everything in this box competes for the same 16 ms.
JSIA thin C++ layer sitting between JS and nativeReplaces the old JSON bridge. Calls are direct and can be synchronous — this is what makes everything below possible.
Fabric (C++ renderer)Scheduler, Shadow Tree, Yoga, diffing, mounting coordinatorWhere a React tree becomes a layout. Lives in C++, shared by both platforms, so layout no longer round-trips through JS.
UI threadReal UIKit / Android views, touch handling, the frame loop — plus the Reanimated UI runtimeOwns the pixels and the gestures. If this thread stalls, the app freezes completely.
TurboModulesCamera, GPS, Bluetooth, sensors — loaded lazily, generated by CodegenSits beside the render path, not inside it. Called on demand, which is why startup got faster.
GPURasterization, compositing, vsyncThe last step. Transform and opacity are cheap here; changing layout is not.

The life of one state update — follow the arrows down:

  • 1. You call setState. The React Reconciler on the JS thread builds a new Fiber tree and works out what changed — exactly like React on the web.
  • 2. The result crosses JSI into C++. No JSON, no queue, no waiting for the next batch.
  • 3. Fabric builds a new Shadow Tree — an immutable snapshot of what the UI should look like. Because it is immutable, unchanged branches are shared with the previous tree instead of copied.
  • 4. Yoga computes Flexbox layout in C++ and fills in x, y, width and height for every node.
  • 5. Diffing compares the old and new shadow trees and produces the smallest set of mutations — create this view, update that prop, delete this one.
  • 6. The Mounting Coordinator commits those mutations to the UI thread, which updates the real native views (Host Components — View, Text, Image, and any custom native view).
  • 7. The GPU rasterizes and composites the frame and shows it at the next vsync — 60 or 120 times a second.
The detail that impresses: the Reanimated UI runtime in the UI-thread box is a second JS runtime. Worklets and shared values live there, so a drag or a spring animation never touches the JS thread at all. That is why a gesture stays at 60 FPS while React is busy rendering a list — it is running on a completely different path through this diagram.

What the same diagram looked like in the old architecture: the JSI box was a bridge — asynchronous, batched, everything serialized to JSON strings. There was no C++ shadow tree shared between sides, all native modules were created eagerly at startup, and Codegen did not exist, so a wrong argument type was a runtime crash instead of a build error. Every problem people remember — blank cells on fast scroll, janky JS animations, slow cold start — comes from that one box.

💬 Say it like this

There are three execution contexts. The JS thread runs Hermes, React and my app logic. The UI thread owns the real native views and draws the frames. Between them sits Fabric, the C++ renderer, reached through JSI instead of the old JSON bridge.

When state changes, the reconciler figures out what changed, that goes through JSI into C++, Fabric builds a new immutable shadow tree, Yoga computes the layout, the diff produces the minimal set of mutations, and the mounting coordinator applies them to the real views on the UI thread. Then the GPU composites the frame.

Two things sit outside that main path. TurboModules are the native APIs — camera, GPS, sensors — loaded lazily on first call instead of all at startup, which is a big part of why the New Architecture starts faster. And Reanimated has its own runtime on the UI thread, so gestures and animations run there directly and never depend on the JS thread being free.

Why is the Shadow Tree immutable?
So a new tree can be built on a background thread while the current one is still being rendered, and then committed atomically. Unchanged branches are shared rather than copied, which makes the diff cheap. It is the same idea as immutable state in Redux, applied to the view tree.
Where exactly does a slow render show up on this picture?
Almost always in the top box — the reconciler doing too much work on the JS thread. Everything below it is C++ and native and is rarely your bottleneck. That is why profiling starts with React DevTools, not with native tools.
What is "bridgeless mode"?
The state shown here: the legacy bridge is gone entirely, not just bypassed. JS calls native through JSI directly, synchronously where needed, with no serialization. Old libraries still run through an interop layer, which is the usual source of upgrade pain.
Why is Skia marked optional?
By default RN draws with the platform's own view system. react-native-skia adds a GPU canvas for custom drawing, shaders and effects — powerful, but an extra dependency, not part of the core pipeline.

topics.title: The render pipeline — Render, Commit, Mount.
topics.html:
This is the official model from the React Native docs. Three phases, and the same three happen both for the very first render and for every update. React itself is unchanged underneath — Fiber, the render phase and the commit phase are all still there; the next card lines the two vocabularies up.

JS C++ Native ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── React Element Tree → React Shadow Tree → Host View Tree (your components) (props + layout) (UIView / ViewGroup) 1. RENDER 2. COMMIT 3. MOUNT build the trees layout + promote diff + apply

First, the three trees. Most of the confusion about this topic is just vocabulary:

TreeWhereWhat it is
React Element TreeJavaScriptWhat your components return. Temporary — it only exists as React's fibers.
React Shadow TreeC++One node per host component, holding props and, after layout, position and size. Immutable.
Host View TreeNativeThe real views: UIView on iOS, android.view.ViewGroup on Android.

Phase 1 — Render. React runs your components until nothing is left to reduce, producing a tree of host components.

  • As it goes, the renderer synchronously creates a Shadow Node in C++ for each host component, through JSI.
  • Only host components get a shadow node. <View> becomes a ViewShadowNode, <Text> becomes a TextShadowNode — but your own <MyComponent> never has one. It is a composite component; it only produces other components.
  • Parent–child links in the element tree are mirrored in the shadow tree. That is how the shadow tree gets built.
function MyComponent() {
  return (
    <View>                      {/* → ViewShadowNode  */}
      <Text>Hello, World</Text> {/* → TextShadowNode  */}
    </View>
  );
}
// <MyComponent /> itself → no shadow node at all

Phase 2 — Commit. Two things happen:

  • Layout calculation — Yoga walks the shadow tree and computes x, y, width and height for every node, using its styles and the space available at the root. Most of it is pure C++, but some components must be measured by the platform itself — Text and TextInput, because only iOS and Android know how their own text engine wraps a line.
  • Tree promotion — the finished tree is marked as the "next tree": the one that will be shown. It is mounted on the next tick of the UI thread.

Phase 3 — Mount. Turning the shadow tree into pixels. Three steps:

  • Tree diffing — compare the previously rendered tree with the next tree, entirely in C++. The output is a list of tiny operations: createView, updateView, removeView, deleteView. View flattening happens here too (see the next card).
  • Tree promotion — the "next tree" atomically becomes the "previously rendered tree", so the next diff compares against the right thing.
  • View mounting — those operations are applied to the real native views, on the UI thread. On the first render there is nothing to compare with, so the list is simply "create everything".
Numbers from the docs that are nice to drop: a real screen is typically 600–1000 shadow nodes, which shrink to roughly 200 real views after flattening. On tablets and desktop it can be ten times more.
💬 Say it like this

The pipeline has three phases: render, commit and mount. Render is React’s normal render phase — the same Fiber work as on the web — and as React finishes each host component, the renderer creates a matching shadow node in C++ — my own components do not get one, only the real primitives like View and Text.

In commit, Yoga computes the layout for that shadow tree, and the tree is promoted to be the "next tree" to show. Text is the interesting exception: it has to be measured by the platform, because only iOS and Android know how their own text engine wraps lines.

In mount, the renderer diffs the previous tree against the next one, gets a small list of operations like createView or updateView, and applies them to the real native views on the UI thread. So a state change does not rebuild the native UI — it produces the minimal set of mutations.

Why does the shadow tree exist at all?
It is a cheap, thread-safe representation of the UI that can be built and measured without touching real views. Real views can only be created on the UI thread; shadow nodes can be created and laid out anywhere.
Where does your slow code actually sit in this picture?
Almost always in the render phase — your components running on the JS thread. Commit and mount are C++ and native and are rarely the bottleneck.
Is this the same as React's render/commit on the web?
The idea is the same — build, then apply. React Native adds a middle layer: an extra C++ tree, plus a layout step with Yoga, because there is no browser to do layout for you.

topics.title: Wait — where is Fiber in all this? Do React's render and commit phases still exist?
topics.html:
Yes, all of it. React Native uses the same react package as the web. What changes is the renderer. Two vocabularies describe the same machine, and mixing them up is what makes this topic confusing.

  • React itself knows nothing about the DOM and nothing about native views. It talks to a renderer through a host config — a set of functions like createInstance, appendChild, cloneInstance, commitUpdate.
  • react-dom is one implementation of that host config. Fabric is another. Same reconciler, same Fiber tree, same scheduler, same priorities.
React's words React Native docs' words ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── render phase (Fiber work) ═══ RENDER ↳ completeWork calls the host config → Fabric creates a C++ ShadowNode commit phase (refs, useLayoutEffect) ═══ COMMIT ↳ + Yoga layout + promote "next tree" (React is finished here) ═══ MOUNT ↳ C++ diff → mutations → UI thread applies them
React's phaseWhat happens in React NativeRN docs call it
Render phase — React calls your components, builds the work-in-progress Fiber tree, interruptible, no side effectsIdentical. And when React finishes a host fiber (View, Text), it calls the host config, and Fabric creates the matching C++ shadow nodeRender
Commit phase — React applies the finished tree, sets refs, runs useLayoutEffect, schedules useEffectIdentical, plus the renderer's own commit: Yoga computes layout and the new tree is promoted to "next tree"Commit
— nothing. React's job is doneFabric diffs the two shadow trees in C++, produces mutations, and the UI thread applies them to real viewsMount

So the short version: RN's Render and Commit are React's render and commit. RN's Mount is below React entirely — React never sees it. On the web there is no equivalent step, because react-dom writes to the DOM directly during commit and the browser handles the rest.

The one real difference: mutation mode vs persistence mode.

// react-dom — mutation mode: change the existing node in place
node.style.backgroundColor = "yellow";

// Fabric — persistence mode: you cannot mutate, so React asks for a copy
cloneInstance(oldShadowNode, { backgroundColor: "yellow" })  // → new node
  • React's reconciler supports both modes. react-dom uses mutation; Fabric uses persistence.
  • That single choice is where the immutable shadow tree and structural sharing from the previous card come from. It is not a separate mechanism bolted on — it is just which mode the host config runs in.

But why can't Fabric just mutate, like the DOM does? This is the part worth being able to explain, because it is the reason for almost everything else in the pipeline.

  • The DOM has one thread; the shadow tree has two. In a browser only the main thread ever touches a DOM node, so mutating in place is safe. In React Native the JS thread is building and measuring a new tree while the UI thread is still mounting the previous one. Changing a node someone else is reading is a data race.
  • Immutable data needs no locks. If nothing is ever modified, two threads can read the same node at the same time with zero synchronisation. That is how the renderer can expose synchronous, thread-safe APIs — and in Fabric it is enforced by the compiler, through C++ const correctness.
  • The swap is atomic. A complete new tree is prepared and then promoted in one step, so the screen never shows a half-updated UI — no frame where the new layout is applied but the new colour is not.
  • Interruptible rendering only works this way. Concurrent React can abandon a half-built tree when something more urgent arrives. If it had been mutating the live tree, abandoning would leave it corrupted. Throwing away an unfinished copy costs nothing.
  • The diff gets cheap. Because untouched branches are literally the same objects in both trees, the C++ diff skips them with a pointer comparison — the same trick as Object.is in React.memo, one level down.

The price is cloning the path from the changed node up to the root. That is one node per level, so it scales with the depth of the tree, not its size — a small, predictable cost in exchange for all of the above.

Two things both called "commit". React's commit phase (refs, layout effects) and Fabric's commit (layout + tree promotion) are neighbours, not the same thing — React's commit is what triggers Fabric's. The RN docs put both under one word, which is exactly where people get lost.

Does React "jump into C++"? No. The host config functions are implemented in C++ and exposed to JavaScript through JSI, so calling one is an ordinary synchronous function call from the JS thread — no serialization, no message queue. Each host fiber simply holds a pointer to its C++ shadow node. And the React Element Tree is not a thing that lives somewhere: it is the fiber tree, a temporary representation, exactly as on the web.

💬 Say it like this

React Native runs the same React. Fiber, the render phase, the commit phase, priorities, Suspense — all of it is there, because it is literally the same react package. Only the renderer is different: on the web it is react-dom, in React Native it is Fabric.

React talks to a renderer through a host config — functions like createInstance and cloneInstance. So when the docs say "the renderer creates a shadow node in C++", that is just React's render phase calling the host config, and Fabric's implementation of it happens to be C++ reachable through JSI. It is a normal synchronous call from the JS thread.

So the mapping is: React Native's Render phase is React's render phase, its Commit phase is React's commit plus Yoga layout, and Mount is extra work that sits below React — diffing the shadow trees in C++ and applying mutations on the UI thread. React never knows that part exists.

The one genuine difference is that react-dom mutates DOM nodes in place, while Fabric runs the reconciler in persistence mode, so React clones nodes instead. And the reason is threads: in a browser only one thread touches the DOM, but here the JS thread is building a new tree while the UI thread is still mounting the previous one. If nothing is ever mutated, both threads can read safely without locks, the new tree can be swapped in atomically, and React can throw away a half-built tree when it needs to interrupt. That is where the immutable shadow tree and structural sharing come from.

So could you write your own React renderer?
Yes — that is what react-reconciler is for. react-three-fiber renders to a 3D scene, Ink renders React to a terminal. You implement the host config; React handles the rest. Knowing this is the cleanest way to show you understand where React ends and the platform begins.
Does useLayoutEffect work in React Native?
It runs, synchronously in React's commit phase, same as on the web. But the native views are mounted on the UI thread afterwards, so it is not a reliable place to read real sizes — use onLayout or the measure callback for that.
Is reconciliation different in React Native?
No. Same rules: same element type and same key means reuse and update, otherwise unmount and recreate. That is why the "never use the index as a key" rule is identical here.
Does the old architecture use Fiber too?
Yes — Fiber is React, not the renderer. The old architecture had the same reconciler; it just sent the resulting UI operations over the async JSON bridge instead of into a C++ shadow tree.

topics.title: What actually happens on a state update? Cloning and structural sharing.
topics.html:
Both trees are immutable, so React cannot just change a colour in place. It has to build a new tree — but it only copies what it has to.

// before: red box + blue box. State changes red → yellow
<View>                                        {/* Node 1 */}
  <View style={{ backgroundColor: "yellow" }} />  {/* Node 3 — changed  */}
  <View style={{ backgroundColor: "blue" }}   />  {/* Node 4 — untouched */}
</View>
  • Render: React clones the node that changed, and every node on the path up to the root — Node 3 → 3', its parent → 2', the root → 1'. Node 4 is not cloned; the old and new trees share it. That is structural sharing, and it is why immutability is cheap here.
  • The rule: a node is cloned only if its props, styles or children changed. Everything else is reused by reference.
  • Commit: layout runs again. One subtlety worth mentioning — a shared node may still get cloned during layout, because if its parent moved, its own position changed too.
  • Mount: the diff between the old tree and the new one produces exactly one operation here: updateView(Node 3, { backgroundColor: "yellow" }). One property on one native view is touched. Nothing is recreated.
  • The renderer can also skip intermediate versions — if several updates land quickly, it can diff the currently mounted tree against the newest one directly.
The link to something you already know: this is the same reason we never mutate state in Redux or React. Immutability plus structural sharing gives you cheap comparisons and safety across threads. Here it is applied to the view tree, in C++.
💬 Say it like this

Because the trees are immutable, a state update does not modify anything — React clones the node that changed plus everything on the path up to the root, and shares every untouched branch with the previous tree. So changing a colour deep in a screen does not copy the whole screen.

Then the diff between the old and the new tree produces the minimal list of mutations — in that example literally one updateView with the new background colour — and only that one native view is touched on the UI thread.

The reason for the immutability is thread safety: the new tree can be built and measured on one thread while the current one is still on screen, and then swapped in atomically.

Is cloning the whole path to the root expensive?
No — it is one node per level, so it is proportional to tree depth, not tree size. The wide, untouched parts are shared. This is exactly how persistent data structures work.
So why do people still say "avoid re-renders"?
Because the expensive part is not this C++ machinery — it is your component functions running on the JS thread in the render phase. The pipeline below them is already minimal.

topics.title: View flattening — why your wrapper <View>s are cheaper than you think.
topics.html:
• Composition means we write a lot of wrappers that exist only to add spacing — a <View style={{ margin: 10 }}> around a card. The docs call these "layout-only" nodes: they affect layout but draw nothing.
  • Conceptually each node becomes one real view, so a deep tree of wrappers would mean a deep, slow native hierarchy.
  • View flattening merges those layout-only nodes into their parent, so no real native view is created for them. The user sees exactly the same screen.
  • It runs as part of the diffing step in the mount phase, in C++, so it costs no extra CPU pass and works identically on iOS and Android.
  • The algorithm looks at props like margin, padding, backgroundColor and opacity to decide whether a node can be flattened. A node that needs its own drawing, touch handling or clipping cannot be.
  • Effect in numbers: ~600–1000 shadow nodes typically collapse to ~200 host views.
💬 Say it like this

A lot of the Views we write exist only to add margin or padding — the docs call them layout-only nodes. If every one of them became a real native view, the hierarchy would get deep and slow.

View flattening merges them into the parent during the diffing step, in C++, so they never become real views. That is why I do not panic about one extra wrapper for spacing. What I do avoid is deep nesting where the wrappers actually draw something — a background colour, a border or a shadow — because those cannot be flattened away.

Then is view nesting free?
No. Pure layout wrappers are cheap; anything with a background, border, shadow, opacity animation or its own touch handler becomes a real view and adds to the hierarchy.
How do you inspect the real hierarchy?
The native inspectors — Android Studio's Layout Inspector or Xcode's View Hierarchy Debugger. They show the host views that actually exist, after flattening.

topics.title: Which phase runs on which thread — and why the render phase can be interrupted.
topics.html:
• The renderer uses two threads: the UI thread, the only one allowed to touch real views, and the JS thread, where the render phase and layout normally run.
  • Thread safety comes entirely from immutability — every update creates or clones objects instead of mutating them, which is what lets the renderer expose synchronous APIs safely.
ScenarioWhat happens
Normal renderRender and commit on the JS thread; mount on the UI thread on its next tick. This is the common case.
High-priority eventThe whole pipeline can run synchronously on the UI thread — for example when a user interaction must be reflected immediately.
Low-priority interruptionAn event on the UI thread interrupts the render phase; its state is merged and rendering continues on the JS thread.
Discrete (high-priority) interruptionThe render phase is interrupted, merged with the event, and finished synchronously on the UI thread.
C++ state updateStarts on the native side and skips the render phase entirely — straight to commit and mount.

What is a C++ state update? Some state is owned by native, not by React. The classic example is ScrollView's scroll offset: it changes on the native side dozens of times a second, and React is not the source of truth for it. So the renderer updates the shadow node directly. Because another commit may land at the same time, it clones the latest committed node, tries to commit, and retries until it succeeds — that is how races are avoided without locks.

This is the concrete payoff of Fabric. In the old architecture everything went through an async, batched bridge, so nothing could be interrupted or made synchronous. Interruptible, priority-aware rendering is exactly what makes React 18 features like startTransition behave correctly on mobile.
💬 Say it like this

There are two threads that matter: the UI thread, which is the only one that can touch real views, and the JS thread, where the render phase and layout usually happen. Mounting always ends up on the UI thread.

The interesting part is that this is not fixed. If a high-priority interaction comes in, the renderer can run the whole pipeline synchronously on the UI thread, and the render phase itself is interruptible — an event can cut into it, the state gets merged, and rendering continues. That is what makes concurrent React work properly here, and it was impossible with the old asynchronous bridge.

There is also one path that skips render completely: state owned by native, like a ScrollView's scroll offset. React is not the source of truth for it, so the renderer clones and commits the shadow node directly, retrying if another commit lands first.

Does this mean layout no longer has its own thread?
Right — the old architecture had a separate shadow thread for layout. In the New Architecture the docs describe two threads, with layout running as part of commit, usually on the JS thread and in C++.
Where does Reanimated fit?
Outside this pipeline. It runs worklets in its own runtime on the UI thread, so an animation or gesture never waits for the render phase at all.
Why does measuring a view need a callback?
Because real size and position only exist after commit and mount. onLayout or measure gives you the value once the pipeline has produced it — you cannot read it during render.

topics.title: Hermes — what is it and why does it matter?
topics.html:
• Hermes is a JavaScript engine built by Meta specifically for mobile. It is the default engine since RN 0.70.
  • The key idea: it compiles your JS to bytecode at build time, not on the user's phone. So the app does not have to parse and compile a megabyte of JavaScript during startup.
  • Result: faster startup (TTI), lower memory use, and a smaller app than shipping JavaScriptCore.
  • Trade-off: Hermes has no JIT. For long, CPU-heavy loops a JIT engine can be faster. For normal app code — UI, network, state — Hermes wins because startup and memory matter more than peak throughput.
  • Because the shipped code is bytecode, crash reports need source maps. Upload the Hermes source map to Sentry/Crashlytics or your stack traces are unreadable.
  • Debugging uses the Chrome DevTools protocol — this is what powers RN DevTools in modern versions.
💬 Say it like this

Hermes is the JavaScript engine RN ships with by default. The big win is that our JavaScript is compiled into bytecode during the build, so the phone does not waste time parsing and compiling it at startup. That gives noticeably faster app launch and lower memory, which is exactly what matters on a cheap Android device.

The one thing to remember in production is source maps — since we ship bytecode, crash reports are useless unless the Hermes source map is uploaded with the release.

When would you turn Hermes off?
Almost never today. Historically for a library that needed JSC, or for very heavy numeric work that benefits from a JIT. If you turn it off you lose startup time and gain app size.
Does Hermes support modern JS?
Yes — modern syntax, async/await natively, and Intl is included now, which used to be a classic Android-only bug with date and number formatting.

topics.title: Which threads does a React Native app use, and what is the 16 ms budget?
topics.html:
• JS thread — runs your React code, effects, state updates, business logic, and any JS-driven animation. Single-threaded, like the browser.
  • UI thread (also called main thread) — owns the real native views. It handles touches, native scrolling, and drawing every frame.
  • Background / shadow work — layout with Yoga. In the old architecture this was a separate thread; in Fabric it happens in C++.
  • 60 FPS means every frame has about 16.6 ms. 120 Hz screens cut that to ~8 ms. If either thread misses the deadline, the user sees a dropped frame.

The diagnostic trick worth memorising:

SymptomWhich thread is busyTypical cause
Scrolling is smooth but rows appear blank, buttons respond lateJS threadHeavy render, big JSON parse, too many re-renders, expensive list items
Everything freezes, even the scrollUI threadHuge images being decoded, very deep view tree, heavy native work, a blocking sync native call
Say this and you sound senior: "First I check the Perf Monitor to see which thread is dropping frames, because the fix is completely different depending on the answer."
💬 Say it like this

There are two threads I care about. The JS thread runs my React code, and the UI thread owns the real views and draws the frames. Each frame has about 16 milliseconds at 60 FPS.

The useful part is that the symptom tells you which thread is the problem. If the list scrolls smoothly but the rows show up empty and taps feel delayed, the JS thread is overloaded — too many re-renders or heavy work in render. If the whole screen freezes including the scroll, the UI thread is blocked, usually by images or a very heavy view tree. So my first step is always the Perf Monitor to see which of the two is dropping frames.

How do you move work off the JS thread?
Reanimated worklets and gesture-handler run on the UI thread. useNativeDriver does the same for the Animated API. Truly heavy computation belongs in a native module or on the server. InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions just delays work until an animation finishes — it does not make it cheaper.
Is there a Web Worker equivalent?
Not built in. The closest options are a second JS runtime via a library, Reanimated worklets for UI-thread code, or pushing the work to native.

topics.title: Styling and layout in React Native — Yoga, Flexbox and the differences from CSS.
topics.html:
Layout is computed by Yoga, a C++ implementation of Flexbox. It is Flexbox, but with different defaults and a smaller feature set.

CSS on the webReact Native
flexDirection: row by defaultflexDirection: "column" by default
position: static by defaultposition: "relative" by default
Cascade and inheritanceNo cascade. Only Text inside Text inherits font styles.
display: block/inline/gridOnly flex and none. No grid, no float, no inline.
px / rem / % / vhPlain numbers = density-independent pixels. % works for width/height/margin/padding. No vh/vw — use useWindowDimensions().
Media queriesuseWindowDimensions() + conditional styles
Shorthand margin: 0 autoNo shorthand strings. marginHorizontal: "auto" or separate keys.
const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  row: { flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", gap: 8 },
  fill: { flex: 1 },
});

// styles compose as an array — later wins, falsy entries are ignored
<View style={[styles.row, isActive && { backgroundColor: "#eef" }, props.style]} />
  • flex: 1 means "take the free space of the parent". It only works if the parent also has a height — an unbroken flex: 1 chain from the root, or an explicit size. A lone flex: 1 inside an auto-height parent does nothing. This is the number one layout bug for beginners.
  • StyleSheet.create is not required any more for performance, but it gives you validation and autocomplete, and keeps style objects out of the render path so they are not recreated every render.
  • Platform-specific styling: Platform.select({ ios: ..., android: ... }), or separate Button.ios.tsx / Button.android.tsx files that you import as ./Button.
  • Shadows used to be the classic split — shadowColor/shadowOffset/shadowOpacity/shadowRadius on iOS, elevation on Android. Modern RN also supports boxShadow, but many codebases still carry the old split.
  • Libraries you may be asked about: NativeWind (Tailwind classes compiled to RN styles), Tamagui, styled-components/native, Unistyles. They all compile down to the same style objects.
💬 Say it like this

Layout in React Native is Flexbox through Yoga, so the concepts transfer from the web, but the defaults are different — the main direction is column, not row, and there is no cascade or inheritance, so every component gets its own style object.

The thing that catches everyone at the start is flex: 1. It only fills the parent if the parent itself has a height, so you need an unbroken chain of flex: 1 from the screen root. Half the "why is my screen empty" bugs are exactly that.

How do you handle different screen sizes and tablets?
useWindowDimensions() re-renders on rotation, unlike a one-time Dimensions.get(). For layout that depends on its own box, onLayout. Percentages and flex over hardcoded pixel values.
What does StyleSheet.create actually do today?
Mostly validation, dev-time warnings and a stable object identity. The old "it sends an ID over the bridge" optimisation is gone, so an inline object is not a performance crime — but it does create a new reference every render, which can break React.memo.
Why does my absolutely positioned element not show on top on Android?
Android stacking uses elevation as well as zIndex. Add elevation, and check that no parent has overflow: "hidden" clipping it.

topics.title: Expo vs bare React Native CLI — which one and why?
topics.html:
• Expo is now the recommended way to start a React Native app in the official docs. It is a framework on top of RN, not a separate platform.
  • What you get: a large set of ready native modules (camera, notifications, secure store, file system), EAS Build (cloud builds, no local Xcode needed), EAS Update (over-the-air JS updates), and Expo Router (file-based navigation).
  • Prebuild generates the ios/ and android/ folders from your app.json, and config plugins let you modify native project files in a repeatable way — so upgrades do not mean re-applying manual native edits.
  • The old objection — "you cannot use custom native code with Expo" — is outdated. With a development build you can use any native library.
  • Bare CLI still makes sense when you have heavy custom native code, an existing native app you are adding RN into, or company rules that forbid cloud builds.
  • Brownfield is the term for embedding RN inside an existing native app — one screen in RN, the rest native. Worth knowing the word.
💬 Say it like this

I default to Expo now, because it is what the React Native docs recommend and it removes most of the painful parts: builds run in the cloud, over-the-air updates are built in, and config plugins keep native changes in code instead of manual edits inside the ios and android folders.

The old reason to avoid Expo — that you could not use custom native modules — is not true any more with development builds. I would still go bare CLI if a project already has a big native codebase or we are embedding React Native into an existing native app.

What is "ejecting"?
An old term. It is now expo prebuild, and it is reversible — the native folders are generated output, not something you hand-edit.
How painful is upgrading React Native?
The JS part is easy; the native folders are the problem. The React Native Upgrade Helper shows an exact diff between versions. Expo smooths this a lot because prebuild regenerates the native projects.
